title: Palliative Pain: Comfort Is an Active Nursing Priority
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: In palliative care, pain relief is a primary goal. Assess pain burden and function, administer the prescribed regimen safely, and escalate uncontrolled pain or adverse effects rather than normalizing suffering.
recognize: Pain may be somatic, visceral, neuropathic, incident-related, or multifactorial and may present through behavior when communication is limited.
priorities: Assess severity, location, quality, triggers, response to prior treatment, sedation, respirations, bowel function, and patient-defined comfort goals.
assessMonitor: Trend pain response, alertness, respiratory status, constipation, nausea, and ability to rest or interact as desired.
interventions: Use prescribed pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic measures and report persistent breakthrough pain for plan adjustment.
medicationSafety: Opioids and adjuvants require monitoring for sedation, respiratory depression, constipation, and interactions; do not independently escalate doses outside orders/protocols.
redFlags: Pain uncontrolled despite prescribed rescue plan
teaching: Reinforce the written breakthrough-pain plan and when to contact hospice/palliative clinicians.
delegationScope: Pain observations can be gathered by trained staff; evaluation of uncontrolled pain and medication response requires licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Withholding ordered analgesia solely because the patient is approaching end of life despite distress and an active comfort plan.
oneLinePearl: Comfort care still requires assessment, monitoring, and escalation.

title: Palliative Dyspnea: Treat Distress, Not Just the Number
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Breathlessness is a subjective distress symptom. Positioning, airflow, calm coaching, prescribed medications, and oxygen when clinically indicated may all contribute; sudden new dyspnea still requires evaluation for reversible danger when consistent with goals of care.
recognize: Tachypnea, accessory-muscle use, anxiety, inability to speak comfortably, new cyanosis, or abrupt change from baseline are important cues.
priorities: Clarify goals of care, assess severity and reversibility, position for comfort, and activate the prescribed symptom plan.
assessMonitor: Trend distress, respiratory pattern, mental status, oxygenation when relevant, and response to interventions.
interventions: Use fan/airflow, upright positioning, reduced exertion, reassurance, and ordered medication/oxygen strategies.
medicationSafety: Opioids/anxiolytics used for symptom relief require individualized orders and monitoring; do not substitute sedation for assessment.
teaching: Teach family the expected comfort plan and which sudden changes require urgent hospice/provider contact.
delegationScope: Basic positioning and observation may be delegated; interpretation of worsening dyspnea requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Chasing a normal oxygen-saturation target when the stated goal is relief of breathlessness and the patient is otherwise comfortable.
oneLinePearl: In palliative dyspnea, symptom relief and goals drive care.

title: Terminal Secretions: Reassure, Reposition, and Follow the Comfort Plan
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Noisy pooled secretions near end of life can distress families more than patients. Reposition gently, provide mouth care, avoid burdensome deep suctioning unless specifically indicated, and use prescribed secretion-management strategies.
recognize: Gurgling upper-airway sounds can occur as swallowing and cough weaken during active dying.
priorities: Assess patient distress, reposition, provide oral care, and explain the finding to family.
assessMonitor: Observe comfort, work of breathing, oral dryness, and response to position or prescribed medication.
interventions: Use lateral positioning, gentle oral suction only when appropriate, and prescribed anticholinergic therapy when ordered.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergic agents may worsen dry mouth, urinary retention, or delirium; use only within the comfort plan.
redFlags: Marked respiratory distress inconsistent with expected dying changes
teaching: Explain that the sound does not automatically mean the patient is suffering or drowning.
delegationScope: Mouth care and repositioning may be shared with trained caregivers/staff; symptom assessment remains licensed oversight.
examTrap: Repeated deep suctioning that causes trauma and distress for expected terminal secretions.
oneLinePearl: Treat the patient’s distress, not the sound alone.

title: Palliative Nausea and Constipation: Prevention Matters
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Constipation and nausea are common from illness, reduced intake/mobility, and medications. Trend bowel pattern and nausea early because untreated symptoms can rapidly worsen comfort and medication tolerance.
recognize: Opioids, anticholinergics, dehydration, obstruction, metabolic changes, and immobility are frequent contributors.
priorities: Assess last bowel movement, stool pattern, abdominal findings, vomiting, intake, medications, and obstruction cues.
assessMonitor: Trend bowel movements, nausea severity, distention, hydration, and response to bowel/antiemetic plans.
interventions: Implement prescribed bowel regimen, hydration/food measures when consistent with goals, and antiemetics as ordered.
medicationSafety: Do not give routine laxatives when obstruction, impaction with overflow, or severe acute abdominal findings are suspected without evaluation.
teaching: Teach caregivers to track bowel pattern when opioids are used and to report persistent nausea or no bowel movement according to the care plan.
delegationScope: Bowel/output observations may be delegated; interpretation and treatment escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Waiting for severe constipation before starting the already-prescribed preventive regimen.
oneLinePearl: Comfort symptoms are easier to prevent than rescue late.

title: End-of-Life Agitation: Look for Reversible Distress First
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Agitation near end of life may reflect pain, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxia, medication toxicity, delirium, fear, or the dying process. Reduce stimulation and assess reversible discomfort before relying on sedating medication alone.
recognize: Restlessness, picking at linens, grimacing, calling out, hallucinations, pulling lines, or sudden behavior change can indicate distress.
priorities: Assess pain, bladder/bowel status, medication changes, respiratory distress, environment, and safety.
assessMonitor: Trend agitation pattern, triggers, level of consciousness, medication response, and caregiver observations.
interventions: Use calm presence, familiar voices, reduced stimulation, repositioning, and prescribed symptom-directed treatment.
medicationSafety: Antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, or sedatives have indication-specific risks; use only under the prescribed palliative plan and monitor response.
teaching: Explain that agitation can be part of dying but should still be assessed for treatable discomfort.
delegationScope: Behavioral observation may be shared; symptom interpretation and medication response require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Assuming every restless dying patient simply needs more sedation.
oneLinePearl: Restlessness is a symptom to assess, not a diagnosis.

title: End-of-Life Mouth Care: Small Interventions Relieve Big Discomfort
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Dry mouth, cracked lips, thick secretions, oral thrush, and inability to swallow can cause substantial suffering. Frequent gentle mouth care is high-value comfort care even when oral intake is minimal.
recognize: Mouth breathing, oxygen flow, anticholinergic medications, dehydration, candidiasis, and reduced intake worsen oral dryness.
priorities: Inspect oral mucosa, lips, tongue, dentition/dentures, swallowing ability, and pain.
assessMonitor: Trend dryness, lesions, coating, bleeding, odor, and comfort after care.
interventions: Provide frequent moistening, lip care, gentle cleansing, denture care, and prescribed treatment for oral infection/pain.
medicationSafety: Avoid products that sting or worsen dryness; swallowing ability must be considered before oral medications/fluids.
teaching: Teach caregivers that comfort mouth care remains important even when eating and drinking decline.
delegationScope: Routine mouth care may be delegated to trained caregivers/staff; abnormal lesions or aspiration risk require licensed review.
examTrap: Stopping mouth care because the patient is no longer eating.
oneLinePearl: When intake fades, mouth care matters more—not less.

title: Palliative Skin Care: Prevent Pain Without Burdensome Routines
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Skin protection remains important, but repositioning frequency and wound goals should be individualized to comfort, tolerance, and overall goals rather than rigid routines that cause suffering.
recognize: Cachexia, immobility, moisture, edema, friction, poor perfusion, and existing wounds increase skin injury risk.
priorities: Assess pain with movement, pressure areas, moisture, wound odor/drainage, and the patient's comfort priorities.
assessMonitor: Trend skin integrity, wound symptoms, pain, and tolerance of repositioning/support surfaces.
interventions: Use gentle repositioning, pressure redistribution, moisture protection, and symptom-focused wound care.
medicationSafety: Time prescribed analgesia to wound care/repositioning when appropriate and monitor sedation.
teaching: Explain that comfort-focused skin care may prioritize symptom relief over wound closure.
delegationScope: Routine turning/skin care may be delegated; wound deterioration and pain require licensed evaluation.
examTrap: Forcing painful scheduled turns without considering the comfort-focused plan.
oneLinePearl: At end of life, skin care protects comfort first.

title: End-of-Life Medication Review: Every Drug Should Still Have a Goal
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: As goals shift toward comfort, some chronic preventive medications may no longer provide meaningful benefit while adding pill burden, interactions, swallowing difficulty, or monitoring burden. The PN/LVN should identify concerns and escalate for prescriber/pharmacy review rather than independently discontinuing therapy.
recognize: Declining intake, dysphagia, renal/hepatic failure, hypotension, sedation, and changing goals can alter medication risk-benefit.
priorities: Reconcile medications and identify those causing burden, duplication, adverse effects, or conflict with current goals.
assessMonitor: Monitor swallowing, alertness, blood pressure, glucose or other parameters as clinically relevant, and symptom benefit.
interventions: Communicate medication-burden concerns to the hospice/palliative prescriber/pharmacist and implement revised orders.
medicationSafety: Do not stop high-risk medications abruptly without clinical review when withdrawal/rebound could cause harm.
teaching: Explain that medication changes reflect changing goals, not abandonment of care.
delegationScope: Medication reconciliation and adverse-effect interpretation require licensed nursing involvement.
examTrap: Independently stopping all chronic medications because the patient enrolled in hospice.
oneLinePearl: Hospice changes medication goals; it does not erase medication safety.

title: Goals-of-Care Handoff: Make the Plan Visible Before Crisis
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Palliative safety depends on clear communication of goals, code status/orders, symptom plans, emergency contacts, and preferred setting of care. A crisis is the wrong time to discover that the team has conflicting assumptions.
recognize: Transitions between home, hospice, facility, ED, and hospital create high risk for lost goals-of-care information.
priorities: Verify current orders/documentation and communicate symptom/escalation plans during every transition.
assessMonitor: Check that family/caregivers understand whom to call, what symptoms to expect, and what interventions align with goals.
interventions: Use structured handoff and ensure copies/access to relevant orders according to law and facility policy.
medicationSafety: Include current comfort medications, last doses, PRN indications, and high-risk adverse effects in handoff.
teaching: Encourage families to keep the hospice/palliative contact plan and current medication list readily available.
delegationScope: Goals-of-care documentation authority varies; PN/LVN should verify and communicate existing orders, not independently establish medical orders.
examTrap: Assuming everyone knows the plan because hospice is involved.
oneLinePearl: A comfort plan only works if every handoff carries it.

title: Actively Dying: Recognize Expected Changes and Unexpected Distress
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Reduced intake, increasing sleep, cooler extremities, mottling, altered breathing patterns, and reduced urine output can occur during active dying. Continue comfort assessment, family support, mouth/skin care, and the prescribed symptom plan while escalating distress that is not controlled.
recognize: Expected dying changes vary; they should be interpreted in context of the documented goals and disease trajectory.
priorities: Assess comfort, pain, dyspnea, agitation, secretions, urinary retention, and caregiver distress.
assessMonitor: Focus monitoring on symptoms that change comfort or management rather than burdensome measurements with no care impact.
interventions: Provide calm presence, mouth care, repositioning as tolerated, prescribed symptom medication, and family education.
medicationSafety: Use the ordered comfort-medication plan and monitor for unintended toxicity while avoiding unnecessary medication burden.
teaching: Explain expected signs of dying and exactly whom to call for uncontrolled symptoms or death according to setting/policy.
delegationScope: Pronouncement and post-death responsibilities vary by state and setting; follow law and facility/hospice policy.
examTrap: Starting burdensome routine monitoring that does not change the comfort plan simply because vital signs are abnormal.
oneLinePearl: Near death, monitor what changes comfort and safety.
